definition: The energy market is a chain of distinct sub-industries (exploration/production, transportation, generation, conversion, and distribution) that together move fuel and power from the ground to end consumers.
core_idea: Because the market is fragmented into specialized sub-industries, most participants only ever see one slice of it, but each slice has its own quirks that a trader still needs to understand alongside the big picture.
key_points: Sub-industries include finding/developing raw fuel sources, transporting them (pipeline, ship), generating power (plants, wind, solar), converting raw materials into finished products, and distributing to consumers (utilities, gas stations).
The energy sector touches nearly every part of the broader economy.
The core of the market is drilling for fuel, building power plants, and running power lines.
The primary commodities are petroleum, natural gas, and electricity, with coal, carbon emissions, nuclear, solar, and wind as secondary/related commodities.
Deregulation turned energy from a purely industrial/operational business into a major financial market on par with stocks and bonds, drawing in Wall Street participation.
relationships: Sets up the physical-vs-financial and spot-vs-forward distinctions discussed later in the chapter.
trading_implications: A trader benefits from understanding both their own niche and how the overall chain connects, since events in one sub-industry (e.g., outages, transport constraints) ripple into others.
